beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Bear. Episode five of five: name what breaks, then ship. This episode covers the failure-mode analysis at ten points, the assembly of all six deliverables, and the quartile bonus at twenty points. The failure-mode analysis is the last skeptical move of the assignment — you stop asking 'does this prompt work?' and start asking 'what is the shape of the error that someone in my role would be most likely to miss?' That is a different question. And the quartile bonus rewards one thing above all else: evidence that you actually ran the work. Let's finish it.

props.command: Identify 2–3 domain-specific failure modes — the errors hardest for someone in your role to catch. Connect them to Discernment (Ch 6) or the Nine Capacities. Then assemble all six deliverables and submit.
props.runningText: the quartile rewards evidence you ran the work — not that you described running it…
output: Failure-mode analysis: 2–3 domain-shaped failure modes, Botspeak-connected
Assembly: six labeled deliverables in one document
Failure Modes (10 pts) + Quartile position determined

beats.act: what a domain-specific failure mode is
beats.narration_text: A domain-specific failure mode is not 'the model might hallucinate.' Every model hallucinates. That is a generic failure mode — it tells the grader nothing about whether you understand what it means to use a model in your specific role. A domain-specific failure mode names the shape of the error that someone in your exact role would be most likely to miss — because of how your professional training works, because of what your workflow pressures you to skip, because of what the output looks like when it is wrong in your field. For a pharmacist reviewing discharge medications: the failure mode is a plausible-looking drug interaction check that misses a contraindication only visible in the patient's renal function data — data the model was not given and did not ask for. That is the shape of the error that kills a patient and that a tired pharmacist under discharge pressure does not catch.

The assignment asks you to connect each failure mode to Discernment from Chapter 6, or to the Nine Capacities from Chapter 2. Discernment has four verification layers: fact, reasoning, framing, and omission. A domain-specific failure mode maps to the layer that would catch it — and the analysis is: why is that layer the hardest for someone in your role to run consistently? For the pharmacist, the renal-function failure is an omission error: the model said nothing false, but it omitted the check that matters. The omission layer requires you to know what is missing — and under discharge-unit pressure, that knowledge is the first thing that degrades. That is the connection. Not 'this relates to Discernment.' 'This is an omission error, caught only by Layer 4, and Layer 4 is the hardest for a time-pressured clinician to run.'

lines: Your failure mode maps to whichever layer would catch it.

beats.narration_text: The submission is one document with six labeled sections, in this order: one, the adapted prompt; two, the Botspeak justification; three, the worked example — output included; four, the five-component specification; five, the adversarial self-critique with the revision; six, the failure-mode analysis. Each section is labeled. No section is missing. Before you submit: read the list and confirm each section is present and contains its actual artifact — not a description of the artifact, not a placeholder, the artifact itself. A missing section is a zero for that component. A section that describes the artifact instead of presenting it costs points. This is the most mechanical check in the assignment. Run it.

lines: One document. Six labeled sections. In order.
§1 — Adapted Prompt: full text, no brackets, every field role-specific.
§2 — Botspeak Justification: causal argument, concepts cited by name and chapter.

beats.narration_text: The quartile bonus is twenty points and it is not graded on a checklist. It is a relative distribution: the top quartile of submissions earns the full twenty, graded down from there. What puts a submission in the top quartile? Evidence. The worked example has output that shows the model's actual behavior in your domain, and commentary that demonstrates you evaluated it against knowledge the model does not have. The adversarial move found something real and produced a revision that would not exist without the attack. The failure modes are shaped like your role — someone outside your field could not have written them. The specification was clearly written before the prompt, not reverse-engineered from it. The justification makes a causal argument, not a vocabulary display. Each of these is a signal. Together they separate a submission that completed the assignment from one that did the assignment.

lines: Worked example: output shows real model behavior; commentary applies knowledge
Adversarial move: found something real; revision would not exist without the attack.

beats.narration_text: Three traps in the failure-mode analysis. First: generic failure modes. 'The model might confabulate' — generic. 'The model might produce a plausible-sounding medication interaction that misses a dose threshold specific to the patient's kidney function' — domain-shaped. Second: only one failure mode with no analysis. The assignment asks for two or three, and it asks you to connect them. One mode with a one-sentence connection is not analysis — it is a label. Third: a missing deliverable. If section three is missing the worked example output, you have already lost eleven points before the quartile calculation. Before you submit, read the document. Confirm each of the six sections contains its artifact. Then submit.

lines: Each one costs points before the quartile sees the submission

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: 'I am writing the failure-mode analysis for my Botspeak Prompt Adaptation. My role is: [your role statement]. My adapted prompt asks the model to: [what your prompt does]. Identify two domain-specific failure modes — errors the model is likely to produce when running this prompt — that someone in my role would be most likely to miss. For each failure mode: name the shape of the error precisely, explain why it is hard to catch given how my role's workflow works, and connect it to the Discernment layer from Botspeak Chapter 6 or a Capacity gap from Chapter 2. Be specific to this role — these failure modes should not apply to adjacent professions.' Read what it produces. If a failure mode could apply to a neighboring role, it is still too generic. Tighten it once more, then assemble and submit.
